section_summary: The section concludes a consular report assessing Japan’s state-supported emigration, particularly plans for strategic settlement in Manchuria and the limited demographic value of migration to Brazil and elsewhere. It includes the report’s source notes, which describe Japanese officials’ growing reluctance to share emigration information with the U.S. Consulate at Kobe. The remaining pages consist of a newspaper clipping and cross-reference sheets concerning proposed overseas settlements, migration and commercial activity in Latin America, settlement in Manchukuo, Japanese migration to the Philippines, and regulations for foreigners in Japan.

subfiles.title: Japanese emigration and colonization policy: conclusion and sources
subfiles.about: The report evaluates Japan’s plans for mass settlement in Manchuria and the broader effectiveness and future direction of government-assisted emigration.
subfiles.summary: The proposed ten-year program would send tens of thousands of families to Manchuria through a government-backed company funded by Japan, Manchukuo, and public or quasi-official investment. The writer considers the scheme primarily a strategic Army project intended to establish soldier-colonists near Russia, but doubts that enough suitable Japanese farmers will migrate or that emigration can materially relieve population pressure. The source note records that Japanese emigration officials and shipping interests became suspicious of the U.S. Consulate’s inquiries, especially after controversy over Brazil’s Couto Amendment, and consequently withheld information.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to report no. 1673: Japan and New Settlements
subfiles.about: The sheet directs researchers to Atherton’s report concerning Daily Herald comments on Japan’s search for new overseas settlements.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: report 1673 from Great Britain on a Daily Herald discussion of Japan and new settlements.

subfiles.title: Japan and New Settlements
subfiles.about: The clipping reports and then questions claims that Japan sought migration rights from Britain, the Netherlands, and other powers for its surplus population.
subfiles.summary: Article: reports Japan prepared approaches for overseas migration; London denied it sought Pacific migration rights; an echo of a Tokyo press campaign tied to Leith-Ross's China mission.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to War Department report on Japanese emigration and commercial penetration of Latin America
subfiles.about: The sheet identifies a War Department report on Japanese emigration and commercial expansion in Latin America.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: War Department report 894.56/78 of March 28, 1935 on Japanese migration and commercial penetration of Latin America.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to report no. 8512 on Japanese settlement in Manchukuo
subfiles.about: The sheet references a military attaché report on a plan to settle five million Japanese in Manchukuo within twenty years.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: report 8512 on a plan to settle five million Japanese in Manchukuo over twenty years and the Tatung Konsu Company regulating laborers from China and Korea.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Nagasaki despatch no. 50 on migration to the Philippine Islands
subfiles.about: The sheet references a Nagasaki despatch concerning Japanese migration to the Philippine Islands and stricter enforcement of Philippine immigration laws.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Nagasaki despatch 50 on Japanese immigration to the Philippines amid stricter enforcement of immigration law.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese Embassy note no. 106 on regulations for foreigners
subfiles.about: The sheet references an embassy note transmitting English translations of Japanese regulations governing foreigners’ entry, residence, trade, travel, and departure.
subfiles.summary: Note 106 included a translation of Home Department Ordinance 6 on foreigners' entry, sojourn and departure and a revision of the entry ordinance.
